1.modern-en: Restless at Baker Street until an anonymous note announces a masked visitor with a matter that could affect the history of Europe.

2.modern-en: Holmes hears Jabez Wilson’s account of the Red-Headed League, a well-paid sinecure for red-haired men that has suddenly dissolved, and sets out to discover what lies behind it.

3.modern-en: Bored by his routine cases, Holmes takes on a young woman’s search for her vanished bridegroom and finds her more interesting than the problem.

4.modern-en: Summoned to Herefordshire to examine a killing by Boscombe Pool, Holmes doubts the overwhelming circumstantial case and sets out to test the accused’s own account.

5.modern-en: Holmes hears John Openshaw’s family history on a stormy night at Baker Street and sets out to explain the orange-pip warnings and protect his client.

6.modern-en: Holmes is already deep in a puzzling disappearance case when Watson’s errand brings the two of them together, and he takes Watson along to help.

7.modern-en: Holmes treats a stray hat and Christmas goose as an intellectual exercise, until something found in the goose turns the puzzle into a serious case.

8.modern-en: Woken early by a frightened client, Holmes takes up a strange case from Stoke Moran in Surrey and sets out to examine the house for himself.

9.modern-en: Holmes hears Hatherley’s account over breakfast at Baker Street and sets out to find where the engineer was taken.

10.modern-en: Holmes takes up a society scandal when a nobleman’s bride vanishes from her own wedding breakfast, working alongside — and against — Lestrade’s official inquiry.

11.modern-en: Holmes takes up the banker’s case and examines the house and the snow-covered grounds at Streatham, doubting the obvious explanation.

12.modern-en: Bored by trivial cases, Holmes is consulted by a governess about an oddly generous offer. He warns her he would not want a sister of his to take the post, and promises to come if she telegraphs.

1.modern-en: Now married and back in medical practice, Watson drops in on his old friend just in time to join the case.

2.modern-en: Watson arrives in the middle of Wilson’s consultation, hears the whole story from the start, and follows Holmes as he looks into it.

3.modern-en: Watson visits Baker Street, tests his own powers of observation on Holmes’s new client, and returns the next evening to hear the outcome.

4.modern-en: Persuaded by his wife to leave his practice for a couple of days, Watson joins Holmes on the train west and narrates the investigation.

5.modern-en: Watson, staying at his old Baker Street rooms while his wife visits her mother, narrates the case.

6.modern-en: Now married and practising as a doctor, Watson sets out late one night on an errand for a friend and is drawn into one of Holmes’s cases.

7.modern-en: Watson calls on Holmes to wish him a happy Christmas and is drawn into following the trail of the goose across London on a freezing night.

8.modern-en: Watson narrates an early case from his bachelor days in Baker Street with Holmes, and goes with him to Stoke Moran.

9.modern-en: Now married and back in medical practice near Paddington, Watson treats the injured engineer and brings him to Holmes. It is one of only two cases Watson ever introduced.

10.modern-en: Watson, a few weeks from his own marriage, has followed the wedding in the newspapers and reads Holmes the reports that set out the case.

11.modern-en: Watson narrates, watches the distraught banker arrive, and accompanies Holmes to Streatham.

12.modern-en: Watson narrates, defends his way of writing up Holmes’s cases, and goes with Holmes to Winchester when Miss Hunter calls for help.

1.modern-en: A retired opera singer, born in America and now living quietly at Briony Lodge in St. John’s Wood. She holds a photograph that a powerful man desperately wants back, and she will not sell it.
The hereditary King of Bohemia, about to make a royal marriage. He needs Holmes to recover a compromising photograph from his past before his betrothal is announced next Monday.

epithet.en: Name given by a masked Bohemian visitor

1.modern-en: The name under which a tall, masked visitor with a German accent introduces himself to Holmes, saying he is a Bohemian nobleman.
A handsome young lawyer of the Inner Temple who visits Briony Lodge every day.

epithet.en: Second daughter of the King of Scandinavia

1.modern-en: A Scandinavian princess of very strict family, engaged to the King of Bohemia.
The coachman who drives Irene Adler’s carriage.

epithet.en: Landlady at Baker Street in this story

1.modern-en: The landlady at Holmes’s Baker Street lodgings.

epithet.en: Clergyman at the Church of St. Monica

1.modern-en: A clergyman at the Church of St. Monica in the Edgeware Road.
Watson’s clumsy servant girl, mentioned in passing.
A well-known actor of the day, mentioned in passing.

2.modern-en: A stout, red-headed pawnbroker from a shabby square near the City. He brings Holmes the story of the Red-Headed League, which paid him £4 a week to copy the Encyclopædia Britannica until it suddenly vanished.
Wilson’s capable young assistant, who works for half wages to learn the trade and spends his spare time on photography. He is the one who shows Wilson the League’s advertisement.

epithet.en: Manager of the Red-Headed League’s office

2.modern-en: The red-headed manager of the League’s office in Pope’s Court, who hires Wilson and sets him to copying the encyclopaedia.

epithet.en: Founder of the Red-Headed League, according to its advertisement

2.modern-en: The late American millionaire whose bequest, according to the advertisement, funds the Red-Headed League.
A Scotland Yard police agent whom Watson already knows; he joins Holmes later in the story.

epithet.en: Sad-faced, respectable gentleman on Holmes’s night expedition

2.modern-en: A gloomy, very respectable gentleman who joins Holmes later in the story and misses his regular Saturday-night game of cards.

epithet.en: Holmes’s client; a short-sighted typist from Camberwell

3.modern-en: A good-natured, short-sighted typist with a small inheritance of her own. Her fiancé vanished on their wedding morning, and she rushes to Baker Street to beg Holmes to find him, vowing to stay true to him whatever happens.

The shy, soft-voiced gentleman Mary met at the gasfitters’ ball and quickly became engaged to. He disappeared from his cab between home and church, leaving behind only a newspaper description and four typed letters.
Mary’s young stepfather, a travelling wine salesman who dislikes her going out. He has refused to involve the police or Holmes in the search for her missing fiancé.
Mary’s mother, a plumber’s widow who has remarried a much younger man. She lives with Mary and her new husband, Mr. Windibank.

epithet.en: Former foreman of the Sutherland family’s plumbing business

3.modern-en: The former foreman of the family plumbing business, who took Mary and her mother to the ball where she met her fiancé.

4.modern-en: A former Australian settler who rents Hatherley Farm from his old colonial acquaintance John Turner. He is the victim whose death beside Boscombe Pool brings Holmes to Herefordshire.
Charles McCarthy’s eighteen-year-old son. The local case points squarely at him, and Holmes is asked to look into it.
The wealthy landowner of Boscombe Valley, who made his fortune in Australia. He is Charles McCarthy’s landlord and old friend from the colonies, and the father of Alice.
John Turner’s daughter, who has known James McCarthy since childhood. Convinced he is innocent, she has engaged Lestrade and, through him, Holmes.
The Scotland Yard detective engaged on the accused man’s behalf. Puzzled by the case, he has passed it to Holmes, though he thinks the facts are plain.
John Turner’s gamekeeper, a witness to the comings and goings near Boscombe Pool on the day of the tragedy.

epithet.en: Daughter of the Boscombe Valley lodge-keeper

4.modern-en: The lodge-keeper’s fourteen-year-old daughter, whose account of what she saw near the pool is a key piece of evidence.

epithet.en: Lodge-keeper of the Boscombe Valley estate

4.modern-en: Keeper of the lodge on the Turner estate, the nearest house to Boscombe Pool.
The official who conducts the inquest and questions the witnesses.
The Italian poet whose work Holmes reads on the train.
The Victorian novelist Holmes proposes to talk about instead of the case.

epithet.en: Young man from Horsham who consults Holmes

5.modern-en: A young man from Horsham who comes to Baker Street on a stormy September night. Strange warnings, five dried orange pips with the letters K. K. K., have followed his family, and one has now come to him.

epithet.en: John Openshaw’s uncle, a former colonel

5.modern-en: John’s uncle, a former Confederate colonel and Florida planter who returned to England and lived as a hard-drinking recluse near Horsham. A letter with five orange pips filled him with terror, and his story is where the family’s trouble begins.
John’s father and Elias’s brother, a retired Coventry manufacturer of bicycle tyres. He laughed at his son’s story of the colonel’s letter.
Three letters, K. K. K., that come with the orange-pip warnings. What they stand for is the first riddle of the story.

epithet.en: Former client of Holmes who sends John to him

5.modern-en: A former client of Holmes who sends John to Baker Street.
The Horsham lawyer Elias Openshaw sends for to witness his will.

epithet.en: Old friend of Joseph Openshaw at Portsdown Hill

5.modern-en: An old friend of Joseph Openshaw who commands a fort on Portsdown Hill.

6.modern-en: Watson’s patient and an opium addict, who has been missing from home for two days. Watson goes to an East End opium den to bring him home.
Isa Whitney’s wife, who comes to the Watsons late at night asking for help to bring her husband back.
Watson’s wife, an old school friend of Kate Whitney. Her kindness brings the night’s first visitor to the door.

epithet.en: Manager of the Swandam Lane opium den

6.modern-en: The man who runs the Bar of Gold, an opium den in Upper Swandam Lane. Holmes knows him as a dangerous enemy.

epithet.en: Mrs. St. Clair’s husband, of Lee in Kent

6.modern-en: A respectable, well-off gentleman of Lee, in Kent, a husband and father, who has vanished. Holmes is investigating his disappearance.
Neville St. Clair’s wife, who saw something alarming in Swandam Lane on the day he disappeared. Holmes is staying at her house, The Cedars, while he works on the case.

epithet.en: The beggar with the twisted lip

6.modern-en: A disfigured beggar with a twisted lip, well known in the City, who lodges at the opium den where Neville St. Clair was last seen.

epithet.en: Police inspector in the St. Clair case

6.modern-en: The police inspector first in charge of the St. Clair inquiry.
A police inspector at Bow Street station who knows Holmes.

9.modern-en: Inspector Bradstreet of Scotland Yard, who joins Holmes in taking Hatherley’s case to Berkshire.

6.modern-en: Isa Whitney’s late brother, a clergyman and college principal; mentioned only.
The writer whose account of opium dreams first tempted Isa Whitney to try the drug.

7.modern-en: A commissionaire known to Holmes. Walking home on Christmas morning, he saw a man attacked by roughs, and was left holding the man’s hat and Christmas goose, which he brought to Holmes.

epithet.en: Owner of the lost hat and goose

7.modern-en: The unknown owner of the battered hat and the goose, traced only by the initials “H. B.” and a card reading “For Mrs. Henry Baker”. Holmes reads a whole life story from his hat.
A titled lady whose famous blue carbuncle was stolen at the Hotel Cosmopolitan. She has offered a large reward for its return.

epithet.en: Plumber charged with the jewel robbery

7.modern-en: A plumber charged with stealing the Countess’s jewel. He has a previous conviction and has been sent for trial, though he protests his innocence.

epithet.en: Upper attendant at the Hotel Cosmopolitan

7.modern-en: An attendant at the Hotel Cosmopolitan whose evidence at the police court describes how the robbery was discovered.

epithet.en: Maid to the Countess of Morcar

7.modern-en: The Countess’s maid, who also gave evidence about the discovery of the robbery.
Landlord of the Alpha Inn near the British Museum, who ran a Christmas goose club for his regulars.

epithet.en: Goose salesman at Covent Garden Market

7.modern-en: A short-tempered goose salesman at Covent Garden Market who supplied the Alpha’s geese.

epithet.en: Egg and poultry supplier in Brixton Road

7.modern-en: A poultry supplier in Brixton Road whose name appears in Breckinridge’s ledger.
The boy who helps at Breckinridge’s stall.

epithet.en: Holmes’s client; Julia Stoner’s twin sister

8.modern-en: A young woman who comes to Holmes at dawn, terrified. She lives with her violent stepfather at Stoke Moran, and is soon to be married, and something she heard in the night has brought her to Baker Street.

epithet.en: Helen Stoner’s stepfather, of Stoke Moran

8.modern-en: Helen’s stepfather, a doctor and the last of an ancient, ruined Surrey family. He is notorious for his ferocious temper, keeps company with gipsies and Indian animals, and Helen still lives under his roof.
Helen’s twin sister. What happened to her two years ago, shortly before her own wedding, is the story Helen brings to Holmes.
Helen and Julia’s mother, who married Dr. Roylott in India and whose money supports the household.
Helen’s fiancé, a friend of many years; their wedding is planned for the spring.

epithet.en: Helen and Julia Stoner’s aunt, near Harrow

8.modern-en: Helen and Julia’s aunt near Harrow, almost the only outside person the sisters were allowed to visit.
A former client of Holmes who recommended him to Helen.

epithet.en: Travellers camped on the Stoke Moran estate

8.modern-en: Wandering gipsies camped on Dr. Roylott’s land, his only friends.
A cheetah that roams the grounds of Stoke Moran, one of Dr. Roylott’s Indian animals.
A baboon that roams the grounds of Stoke Moran, one of Dr. Roylott’s Indian animals.

9.modern-en: A young, struggling hydraulic engineer who turns up at Watson’s surgery at dawn with a terrible hand wound. Watson brings him straight to Holmes to tell his strange story.
A gaunt, German-accented colonel who offers Hatherley a large fee for one night’s work on a hydraulic press in the country. His one condition is absolute secrecy.

epithet.en: Woman Hatherley meets at the house

9.modern-en: A frightened woman Hatherley meets at the remote house where the colonel takes him.

epithet.en: Introduced as Stark’s secretary and manager

9.modern-en: A stout, silent man introduced to Hatherley at the house as the colonel’s secretary and manager.

epithet.en: Missing hydraulic engineer in an old advertisement

9.modern-en: A hydraulic engineer whose disappearance a year earlier Holmes recalls from an old newspaper advertisement.

epithet.en: Paddington railway guard, Watson’s former patient

9.modern-en: A grateful railway guard, once Watson’s patient, who brings Watson new patients from Paddington.
The station-master at Eyford, who gives the party local news when they arrive.
A plain-clothes policeman who accompanies Inspector Bradstreet.

epithet.en: Holmes’s noble client; second son of the Duke of Balmoral

10.modern-en: A proud aristocrat, second son of the Duke of Balmoral, who comes to Holmes after his American bride vanishes from their wedding breakfast. He wants his wife found and the scandal ended.

epithet.en: American heiress; only daughter of Aloysius Doran

10.modern-en: The only daughter of a Californian mining millionaire, freshly married to Lord St. Simon. She disappeared from the wedding breakfast within minutes of the ceremony, and nobody knows where she went.

epithet.en: Former danseuse at the Allegro; longtime friend of Lord St. Simon

10.modern-en: A former dancer and longtime friend of Lord St. Simon who made a scene at the wedding breakfast. The police suspect her in the bride’s disappearance.

epithet.en: Hatty Doran’s father; Californian mining millionaire

10.modern-en: Hatty’s father, a self-made Californian mining millionaire who has brought his daughter to London and hosted the wedding breakfast.
Hatty’s American maid from California, the last person the bride confided in before she vanished.
Lord St. Simon’s father, whose family name and finances hang over the match.

epithet.en: Friend who recommended Holmes to Lord St. Simon

10.modern-en: The nobleman who recommended Holmes to Lord St. Simon.

epithet.en: Senior partner of the bankers Holder & Stevenson

11.modern-en: A wealthy London banker who has accepted the priceless Beryl Coronet as security for a loan to an illustrious client. He rushes to Baker Street in despair after the coronet is damaged in his own house.
Holder’s only son, charming but in debt from gambling, and caught up in the night’s events at the family home in Streatham.

epithet.en: Alexander Holder’s niece and adopted daughter

11.modern-en: Holder’s niece and adopted daughter, who manages his household and is devoted to her uncle.
Arthur’s older, worldly friend, a charming visitor to the Holder house whose influence Holder distrusts.

epithet.en: Second waiting-maid in the Holder household

11.modern-en: A recently hired, pretty waiting-maid in the Holder household who has admirers hanging about the house.

epithet.en: Greengrocer who delivers to the Holder house

11.modern-en: The local greengrocer who delivers to the Holder house.

epithet.en: Exalted borrower who pledged the Beryl Coronet

11.modern-en: A borrower of the highest rank, never named, who leaves the Beryl Coronet with Holder as security for a large loan.

epithet.en: A London governess; Holmes’s client in this story

12.modern-en: A young governess with no family to advise her. She asks Holmes whether to accept a Hampshire post that pays far above the usual rate but comes with strange conditions, including cutting off her hair.

epithet.en: Owner of the Copper Beeches near Winchester

12.modern-en: A stout, jovial gentleman from the Copper Beeches near Winchester. He offers Violet Hunter a generous salary to teach his small son, provided she humours his family’s odd whims.
Rucastle’s much younger second wife, pale and silent. Violet is told that the job’s peculiar requests are her fancies.

epithet.en: Jephro Rucastle’s daughter by his first marriage

12.modern-en: Rucastle’s grown daughter by his first marriage. Her father says she has gone to Philadelphia; the electric-blue dress Violet is asked to wear belonged to her.
The Rucastles’ spoiled six-year-old son and Violet’s charge, whose favourite amusement is hurting small creatures.

epithet.en: Groom and manservant at the Copper Beeches

12.modern-en: The Rucastles’ hard-drinking groom and manservant, the only one who can manage the house’s fierce mastiff.

epithet.en: Toller’s wife; servant at the Copper Beeches

12.modern-en: Toller’s tall, sour-faced wife, the household’s other servant.
Rucastle’s huge, half-starved mastiff, let loose in the grounds every night.
The manager of the West End governess agency where Violet meets her prospective employer.
